results.title: PROBAST: A Tool to Assess Risk of Bias and Applicability of ...
results.content: [Box 3](https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M18-1377#f3-M181377) gives examples of potential review questions for both prognostic and diagnostic prediction models where PROBAST is applicable. For example, such concerns may arise when participants in the prediction model study are from a different medical setting from the targeted population defined in the review question ([Table 2](https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M18-1377#t2-M181377)). Most prediction model studies do not report information on blinding of predictor assessment to outcome data ([121](https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M18-1377#r121-M181377), [122](https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M18-1377#r122-M181377)). Similarly, as in domain 1, in reviews that aim to estimate the average predictive performance of a specific model, heterogeneity in the observed performance of that model across the development study and validation studies is expected due to differences in the definition and measurement of predictors ([17](https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M18-1377#r17-M181377), [40](https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M18-1377#r40-M181377), [44](https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M18-1377#r44-M181377)). *   [PROBAST: A Tool to Assess the Risk of Bias and Applicability of Prediction Model Studies](https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/abs/10.7326/M18-1376). ###### [PREVIOUS ARTICLE Catheter Ablation of Atrial Fibrillation in Patients With Heart Failure Previous](https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M18-0992)###### [NEXT ARTICLE PROBAST: A Tool to Assess the Risk of Bias and Applicability of Prediction Model Studies Next](https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M18-1376).

results.title: Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering for Data Mining: Techniques, Tools, and Best Practices
results.content: *   [Conceptual Framework: A Context-Aware Taxonomy of Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/6/10/257#sec2-ai-06-00257). Preprocessing involves a set of operations, including data cleaning, transformation, normalisation, feature encoding, and DR [[1](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/6/10/257#B1-ai-06-00257),[4](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/6/10/257#B4-ai-06-00257)]. For example, in [[5](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/6/10/257#B5-ai-06-00257)], the authors discuss how various ML pipeline stages can introduce or mitigate bias, while preprocessing facilitates automation within the data pipelines, further contributing to increased reproducibility, scalability, and transferability in application scenarios. We propose a unifying framework ([Section 2](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/6/10/257#sec2-ai-06-00257)), which systematically organises data preprocessing and feature engineering into five pipeline stages (cleaning, transformation, construction, selection, reduction), while explicitly linking them to decision criteria (dataset size, interpretability, domain constraints, computational resources). Because there is no domain-agnostic standard, we adopt a task-driven protocol: (i)diagnose influence (e.g., leverage, Cook’s distance) and distinguish data errors from rare-but-valid events [[42](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/6/10/257#B42-ai-06-00257)]; (ii) compare treatments—retain, transform (e.g., log/winsorise) or remove—using CV on task metrics (ROC-AUC, RMSE) and stability across folds; (iii) select the least complex treatment that improves performance without degrading calibration or fairness; (iv) document decisions and parameters for audit [[24](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/6/10/257#B24-ai-06-00257),[38](https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/6/10/257#B38-ai-06-00257)]. results.title: Automated cell annotation and classification on histopathology for spatial biomarker discovery | Nature Communications
results.content: # Automated cell annotation and classification on histopathology for spatial biomarker discovery. Here, we present an experimental and computational approach for automated cell annotation and classification on H&E-stained images. Instead of human annotations, we use multiplexed immunofluorescence (mIF) to define cell types based on cell lineage protein markers. By co-registering H&E images with mIF of the same tissue section at the single-cell level, we create a dataset of 1,127,252 cells with high-quality annotations on tissue microarray cores. A deep learning model combining self-supervised learning with domain adaptation is trained to classify four cell types on H&E images with an overall accuracy of 86%-89%, and the cell classification model is applicable to whole slide images. We then co-register H&E with mIF images at the single-cell level to establish the ground truth of cell type labels on H&E, which are used to train a deep learning model for classifying four major cell types in the tumor microenvironment.
